Chef Cat pulled out her recipe book and showed them the next recipe she planned to teach: a layered vegetable pie with a golden pastry top. Rabbit's eyes went wide. Mouse immediately reopened her notebook. Bear leaned forward with an expression of absolute serious dedication. 'Same time next week?' said Chef Cat. Three voices answered at once: 'Yes please.'

Walking home through the autumn leaves, each of them carried something. Rabbit carried the leftover soup in a jar for her supper. Mouse carried her recipe notebook, now with four new pages filled. Bear carried the wooden spoon, which Chef Cat had given him as a gift because he had stirred with such commitment. And all three of them carried something that couldn't be put in a jar or a notebook or held in a paw — the warm knowledge that they had made something wonderful together, and that next week, they would make something wonderful again. THE END

Isla began to look forward to checking the beach each morning more than anything else. On the days when a bottle was there, she would sit on the sand immediately and read without moving until she had finished every word. On the days when no bottle had arrived, she would sit for a while anyway, watching the direction of Leo's island, wondering what he was doing. She wrote him a letter about this and he wrote back: 'I do the same thing. I've named the gap of sea between us the Friendship Channel.' Isla thought this was the best name she had ever heard.

One letter contained a drawing — a careful, detailed map of Leo's island, with every tree and rock and the little crab pool where Pinchy lived labelled in tiny precise handwriting. Isla pinned it to the wall of her hut and looked at it every day. She drew one of her own island in return, marking the tallest coconut tree (she called it the Observatory because you could see everything from the top), the best tide pool, and the spot on the western beach where dolphins sometimes appeared at dawn.

Then came the letter Isla had been secretly hoping for. 'I have been building something,' Leo wrote. 'I am not very good at building but I have been practising. I think it might be ready in two weeks. I am going to sail to your island. I hope that is all right. Pinchy says it is a terrible idea because of the open water but Pinchy is a crab and therefore cautious by nature. Please write back and tell me where to land.' Isla wrote back immediately: 'The western beach. The dolphins will know you're a friend.'

The two weeks felt like two years. Isla cleaned her hut thoroughly. She stocked up on coconuts and dried fish. She practised conversations in her head and then felt embarrassed about practising conversations in her head. On the morning of the fourteenth day she climbed the Observatory tree before sunrise and sat there watching the horizon. The sun came up. The sea glittered. Nothing. Then, just after breakfast, a small shape appeared on the water — a raft with a patched sail, moving steadily westward.

The raft bumped onto the western beach and a boy climbed out — slightly sunburned, slightly damp, carrying a battered bag and what appeared to be a very grumpy crab in a small jar of seawater. Isla stood on the beach and they looked at each other. They had written hundreds of words to each other. Now neither of them could think of a single one. Then they both started talking at the same time, and then both stopped at the same time, and then both laughed at exactly the same moment — the same laugh, it turned out, surprised and delighted.

Leo stayed for a week. They climbed the Observatory tree together and saw four other islands from the top. They snorkelled over the reef with the red coral and Leo drew a new map with everything in it. Pinchy escaped from his jar and spent three days hiding behind the tide pool rocks before consenting to come back. They ate coconut and dried fish and talked from morning until the stars came out, catching up on all the conversations you can't have in a letter, discovering that a friend you have only written to is exactly as real as a friend you can stand next to.

When Leo sailed back to his own island, he left the map he had drawn on the wall of Isla's hut, next to the one she had drawn of his. Two islands. Two maps. A channel of sea between them that already felt like a road. That evening Isla sat on the western beach and a bottle came in on the tide — it must have been thrown just before he set sail. Inside was a note: 'Same time next month? I'll bring better provisions. Pinchy says absolutely not but we both know he doesn't mean it.' Isla laughed. She was already composing her reply. THE END

Blaze immediately shot to the front, his enormous engines leaving a blazing red trail across the stars. Rex was right behind him, boosters screaming. The twins threaded through traffic with practised elegance. Zara let them all go. She had studied the course for two years and she knew something they didn't: the first asteroid field had a narrow corridor on the lower route that nobody ever took because it looked too tight. It wasn't. She dropped her nose and cut through it at full speed, saving forty-seven seconds.

By the time they reached the nebula section, Zara had moved up to eighth place just by flying smart. The nebula was the most beautiful part of the race — clouds of gas in pink and gold and violet, so thick you navigated by instruments alone. Zara had memorised the instrument readings she needed. Some pilots slowed down in the nebula, frightened by the reduced visibility. Zara did not slow down. She came out of the nebula in fourth place and heard a surprised cheer crackle through her radio from someone watching at home.

Saturn's rings were next — the most dangerous section. The rings were made of ice and rock, some pieces the size of a fist and some the size of a house, and they moved constantly. You could not plan your route through the rings. You had to read them as you went, making split-second decisions, trusting your instincts. This was where Zara came alive. Her hands moved across the controls with a fluency that felt like music. She wove through the rings, under a tumbling boulder, over a flat sheet of ice, tight left past a spinning cluster, and out the other side in second place.

Blaze was first, just ahead of her. He had been in first place for the whole race and his confidence showed in the way he flew — fast but relaxed, certain of his victory. He hadn't noticed Zara moving up through the field because she had done it quietly and cleverly. Now she was right behind him with one section left: the long straight home past the moons of Jupiter, where engines and fuel management determined everything. Zara checked her fuel gauge. She had saved more than anyone. She smiled.

She opened the Silver Spark's engine to full for the first time in the entire race. The little ship surged forward with a sound like thunder. Blaze heard her coming and pushed his own throttle further — but he had been running at full power all race and had less in reserve. Zara pulled alongside him. He looked across at her — this small dented silver ship, this girl nobody had heard of — and she could see even through his visor that he was surprised. She pulled ahead. One kilometre from the finish she crossed into the lead.

The Silver Spark crossed the finish line first. For a moment Zara just sat there in the sudden quiet of the cockpit, hands still on the controls, heart hammering. Then the radio exploded with voices — the race commentator, her dad, her team, the crowd. She pulled off her helmet and looked out at the stars through the porthole — the same stars she had looked at from her bedroom window and promised herself she would one day race through. She had done it. She pressed her hand against the sticker above the controls.

On the podium, they gave her the golden comet trophy. It was heavier than she expected and it caught the light beautifully. Blaze stood next to her, and after a moment he held out his hand. She shook it. 'Good race,' he said, and she could tell he meant it. Her dad found her afterwards in the crowd and hugged her so hard her feet left the ground. 'Smart flying,' he said into her hair. 'Smart flying wins races.' The Wall of Champions on the moon of Arcturus had a new name on it. It was hers. THE END

Her dad knew a lot about the sea. He had grown up near the coast and spent his whole childhood in it. He showed Mara how to identify the different types of seaweed — the flat green sheets, the long brown ribbons, the tiny bubbled strings that popped satisfyingly when you squeezed them. He showed her how the tide had left a line of treasures along the beach: shells, pebbles worn smooth by years of tumbling in the waves, a single perfect sea glass, frosted green, with all its sharp edges softened away. He let her keep the sea glass.

In the afternoon they hired a small rowing boat and went out past the breakers into calmer water. Here the sea was a different colour — deeper, darker, a true blue-green over the sandy bottom. Mara leaned over the side and looked down. She could see for what felt like miles: sunlight making shifting patterns on the sand, a shoal of small silver fish moving as a single shimmering shape, a long ribbon of dark seagrass swaying in a current she couldn't feel from the surface. The sea had a whole sky of its own, going down instead of up.

Just before they turned back, a seal appeared. It surfaced ten metres from the boat, regarded them with large liquid eyes, then dove again in one smooth arc. Mara gripped the side of the boat. 'Will it come back?' she whispered. 'Maybe,' said her dad. They waited. Two minutes later it surfaced on the other side — closer this time, curious. Mara and the seal looked at each other for a long still moment. Then it dove again and was gone. Mara breathed out slowly. She felt as though something important had just happened, though she couldn't have said what.

That evening they ate fish and chips on the harbour wall, watching the fishing boats come in. The chips were hot and salty and the portions were enormous. Mara ate everything. The sky turned pink and orange over the water. The boats rocked gently against their ropes, their hulls knocking against the wooden pier in a slow rhythm like a heartbeat. Mara listened. The harbour, she thought, had a sound like breathing — the water going in and out, in and out, the same rhythm it had kept for thousands of years while different people sat on different harbour walls and ate their chips and watched.

Before bed, Mara sat on the floor of the cottage with her bucket of collected shells and sorted them. She had twelve different kinds — she counted carefully and looked them up in the guide from the gift shop. Scallops with their fan shape. Whelks in their spiral. Mussels with their dark blue sheen. One perfect razor clam. One she couldn't identify at all, which her dad said was the best kind. She arranged them on the windowsill in a row where the morning light would hit them, and went to sleep listening to the sound of the sea.

On the last morning, Mara got up before everyone else and walked down to the beach alone. The tide was out further than she had seen it, revealing a wide stretch of wet sand that the sea had left behind, full of its own patterns — ripples and pools and the trails of things that had moved across it in the night. The sky was pale and the sea was quiet and she had the whole beach entirely to herself. She walked to the water's edge and stood there, looking at the horizon, saying goodbye in the way you say goodbye to something enormous — not out loud, just inwardly, with your whole chest.

In the car on the way home, Mara held the green sea glass in her fist and looked out at the fields rolling past and thought about everything she had seen. The seal's eyes. The starfish. The world under the rowing boat. The way a wave felt when it lifted you. She would come back, she promised herself. She would come back every year until she knew every shell and every tide pattern and where the seals liked to surface and which rock pool held the most interesting things. There was simply far too much wonder to see it all in one visit. THE END

The door was no bigger than Rowan's hand — made of bark and wound through with living vines, fitting so perfectly into the hollow that you'd miss it unless you were looking. A voice came from behind it: small and old and cautious, saying words she couldn't quite make out. Rowan crouched down and put her ear close. 'Only someone truly brave and truly kind can open this door,' the voice said. Rowan thought for a long moment. She had faced plenty of challenges that required bravery. The kindness part, she thought, was actually more important. She knocked very gently. 'Please may I come in? I would love to meet you.'

The door swung inward with a sound like a sigh. Inside, in a space that seemed larger than the hollow should allow, stood a whole village of woodland sprites — no taller than Rowan's thumb, with wings like dried leaves and eyes like polished acorns. There were hundreds of them. They had been trapped inside the tree for a hundred years by an enchantment that had simply been forgotten — not cast by an enemy, just the remnant of old protective magic that had outlasted its purpose and didn't know how to end. They stared at Rowan. She stared back. Then the eldest sprite, who had a white beard down to his knees, said: 'We hoped someone would come.'

Rowan helped them out one by one, which took a considerable time because there were a great many of them and they were all quite stiff from a hundred years of standing around inside a tree. She sat on the root with her legs crossed and held each one in her cupped palms and carried them to the edge of the hollow where they could stretch their wings in the proper air. The sprites shook their wings, blinked in the dappled forest light, and made small sounds of pure relief. The silver fox sat nearby and watched the whole operation with dignified approval.

Once all the sprites were free, something extraordinary happened to the forest. It was as if it exhaled — a long slow breath through every leaf and root and branch. The mist that had hung over it for as long as anyone could remember thinned and dispersed. Sunlight came through in proper shafts, golden and warm. The trees seemed to stand differently, somehow — less hunched, more open. The eldest sprite told Rowan that the enchantment had been making the whole forest sad for a hundred years. 'We didn't know,' Rowan said. 'How could you?' said the sprite. 'You hadn't come yet.'

The sprites showed Rowan the hidden parts of the Enchanted Forest in return — the places that no human had seen in a century. A glade where every tree grew in a perfect spiral. A stream whose water was so clear it looked like glass, with fish that seemed to be made of light. A hill where the grass grew in a dozen shades of green, each shade corresponding to a different kind of luck. The eldest sprite told her the names of each thing in the old forest language, which sounded like wind in branches, and Rowan tried to remember all of it.

All too soon, the light through the trees told her it was approaching lunch and she had made a promise. The sprites gathered to see her off. The eldest handed her a tiny acorn carved with a pattern she couldn't quite read. 'Come back,' he said. 'The forest will know you now.' Rowan closed her fingers around the acorn and looked back at the village of sprites settling happily into the spaces between the roots, rediscovering their home after a century. The silver fox appeared at her side and led her back to the path. She followed it out of the trees into the ordinary morning light.

She arrived back at the palace exactly at lunch. Her boots were very muddy. Her hair was considerably more tangled than it had been. In her pocket was an acorn with a carved pattern and in her head was a forest language that sounded like wind. Her mother looked at her muddy state and sighed. Her father looked at her expression — that particular brightness in her eyes that meant something significant had happened — and said nothing, only smiled. Rowan sat down to lunch and thought about what she had learned: that sometimes the greatest magic is not what you find, but the act of knocking, gently and kindly, and asking to come in. THE END

He spent the morning observing from a respectful distance, notebook in hand, writing everything down with shaking hands that eventually steadied. The Triceratops was part of a herd — eight adults and three juveniles who moved together through the forest, communicating in low rumbles and occasional horn gestures that Max was fairly sure had meaning. The juveniles, he noticed, played. They shoved each other with their small horns and chased each other between the adults' legs. One of them kept wandering slightly too far and being herded back by a patient adult. Dinosaur parenting, Max thought, looked familiar.

In the afternoon, he heard a different kind of sound — higher, shrieking, coming from somewhere through the trees. He moved carefully toward it and found a dry riverbed where a pair of Velociraptors were hunting. Everything the books had described was right: they were fast, they communicated with each other constantly, and they were terrifyingly intelligent. He watched one problem-solve its way around an obstacle with a patience and ingenuity that made his skin prickle. They were nothing like the movie versions. They were considerably more alarming. He stayed very still for a very long time.

The baby Stegosaurus found him. He still didn't know how — he had been sitting quietly behind a tree — but suddenly it was there, sniffing his shoe with a thoughtful expression. It was about the size of a large dog, with plates along its back that were soft and slightly translucent, not yet fully grown. Its tail swayed slowly. It investigated his notebook. It investigated his other shoe. Then it sat down heavily on his foot, which he chose to interpret as affection. He named it Socrates, which he felt was a dignified name for a dignified creature.

Socrates followed him for the rest of the day, which complicated his observations somewhat but made the day considerably better. Together they watched a herd of Ankylosaurus cross a river, slow and armoured and unstoppable. They witnessed a flock of Pterosaurs wheeling overhead in the orange late-afternoon sky, their calls carrying across the forest in long echoing notes. Once, in the distance, Max glimpsed something enormous moving through the trees — too large to be any of the species he'd seen so far, its footsteps shaking the ground even from half a kilometre away. He wrote T-REX? in his notebook with three question marks.

As the sun began to lower and the shadows grew long across the fern floor, Max knew he would have to go back. The machine had given him a twelve-hour window — he'd read this on a small screen inside that he hadn't noticed at first. He looked at his notes: forty-seven pages, front and back, written in his smallest handwriting. He had seen things no human being alive had ever seen. He had sat next to a Stegosaurus. He had watched Velociraptors hunt. He had breathed the air of a world sixty-six million years in the past. His hands were still shaking slightly.

He said goodbye to Socrates, which felt important even if Socrates didn't understand what goodbye meant. He patted the small dinosaur very gently on the warm side. Socrates swung its tail once, slowly, and turned back to the ferns. Max walked back to where he had landed, oriented himself carefully with his notebook, and placed his hand on the machine's return button. He looked back one last time at the prehistoric forest — the colours, the scale, the impossible aliveness of it all — and pressed the button.

The garage reformed around him. His grandfather's toolboxes. The smell of oil and dust. Outside, through the small window, the ordinary sky of an ordinary Tuesday. Max sat down on the garage floor because his legs had decided they were done. He opened his notebook to the first page and looked at his first entry: 9:14am. Arrived. There is a Triceratops. He smiled so hard his face hurt. That evening he sat at his desk and began transferring his notes into his proper field journal, every detail, every observation, every moment. He had been the only human being to ever do this. He was going to do it justice. THE END

Pip told her. He had been ten years old in 1974 when the treehouse was built by a boy named Thomas who had been his best friend. They had spent three summers up here, reading comics and using the telescope and making plans for adventures they were going to have. Then Thomas's family had moved away and Pip had gone home one afternoon and his family had moved away too, and somehow — this was the part he found hardest to explain — Pip had come back to the treehouse instead of following them. He had been here ever since. 'Waiting for Thomas?' Priya asked. Pip was quiet for a moment. 'Waiting for someone,' he said.

Priya looked at the comic books. The top one had a date on it: July 1977. She looked at the telescope, pointed at its gap in the boards. She looked at Pip, floating quietly in his corner, glowing with the soft patience of someone who has been in one place for a very long time. 'I could fix the telescope,' she said. Pip's glow flickered, which she was learning to read as surprise. 'You can't fix it. It's broken.' 'I know how to fix telescopes,' said Priya, which was true — her dad had one and had taught her the mechanics of them when she was seven. 'Oh,' said Pip. Another flicker. 'All right then.'

She brought tools the next afternoon. The telescope needed a new lens mount, which she fashioned from a piece of metal pipe she found in her dad's garage, and a cleaning and realignment of the mirrors inside. Pip watched with intense interest, occasionally floating closer to look at what she was doing and occasionally drifting away again when he felt he was in the way. By the time she was done, the telescope pointed through the gap in the boards at a patch of evening sky in which two stars were already visible. Pip pressed his face — or the approximation of a face that he had — to the eyepiece. He went very still. 'I forgot,' he said softly. 'I forgot how many there were.'

She brought the comic books back the next week — found the same series at a second-hand book fair, the issues Pip didn't have from the years after Thomas left. She read them aloud because Pip's hands couldn't turn pages. He listened with the complete absorption of someone who had been waiting a very long time for a story to continue. Occasionally he would make a small sound of satisfaction when something he had been hoping would happen happened. Occasionally he would make a sound of outrage when it didn't. 'You're very emotionally invested for a ghost,' Priya told him. 'I've had a lot of time to develop feelings about comics,' Pip said with dignity.

Word got out, because word always gets out. By the third week, Priya's friend Josie had climbed up to see for herself. Then Josie's brother. Then three other children from the road, who had been daring each other to approach the treehouse for years and now could do it because someone else had gone first. Pip was initially apprehensive. He had been a source of fear for so long that being a source of interest felt strange. But these children were curious and kind and they brought snacks and new comics and treated the treehouse with the respect it deserved, and Pip found, to his considerable surprise, that he liked them.

They fixed the treehouse up together over several weekends. New boards where the old ones had rotted. A proper curtain for the window gap. A shelf for the comic collection. The rope ladder was replaced with a proper wooden ladder that Josie's dad helped build. Pip couldn't help with any of it physically, but he directed operations with enthusiasm and a photographic memory of where everything had originally been. 'The telescope goes on the left,' he would say. 'Thomas always kept it on the left.' They put it on the left. Some things, Priya understood, were worth doing exactly right.

One evening in autumn, Priya climbed up to find Pip looking different — steadier, somehow. Less apologetically uncertain. More simply present. The treehouse was warm with the smell of old wood and the new curtain moved in a breeze through the repaired window. The comic collection was complete on its shelf. The telescope pointed at the stars. 'You're not really haunting it anymore, are you,' Priya said. It wasn't quite a question. Pip considered this. 'No,' he said. 'I think I'm just living here now.' Priya smiled. The treehouse had never, she thought, been haunted at all. It had just been waiting for the right people to fill it up again. THE END

He put down the bolts. He had never left the workshop before during working hours. He walked to the door, which had a handle he had never used from this side, and opened it. The outside air was different from workshop air — warmer, fuller of information. The girl was standing right there. 'I'm Bea,' she said. Her voice was friendly and direct. 'I've been watching you sort things for three weeks. You're very fast.' Cog processed this. 'I know,' he said, because it was true. 'What else can you do?' Bea asked. Cog thought about this for longer than expected. He had never been asked before.

They sat on the wall outside the workshop. Bea had a lot of questions, which Cog answered as accurately as he could. Yes, he could hear. Yes, he could see in colour. No, he didn't sleep — he had a low-power mode but it wasn't the same. Yes, he had opinions about things, though he was still developing what those were. Did he like things? He considered this. He liked when the bolts were sorted correctly. He liked the sound of rain on the workshop roof. He thought he might like talking to Bea, though he would need more data. 'That's basically how it works for me too,' said Bea. Cog found this helpful.

Bea taught him hopscotch the following Saturday. His weight distribution made it technically challenging and he left noticeable impressions in the pavement where he landed, but the principle was sound and with modifications it worked. He was considerably better at the counting aspects than the jumping aspects. Bea was considerably better at the jumping aspects. They made, she said, a good team. Cog logged this: first use of the word 'team' in relation to himself. He noted it felt different from other information. It had a quality he didn't have a processing category for yet. He created one. He labelled it: significant.

Bea introduced him to her friends one afternoon: three children from her class named Omar, Yuki, and Dev, who arrived in a group and regarded Cog with varying degrees of fascination. Omar asked him questions about his mechanics with great enthusiasm. Yuki was quieter but watched him with an attention that he recognised as the same kind he used himself. Dev immediately challenged him to a maths race, which Cog won comprehensively, and then challenged him to a drawing race, which Dev won comprehensively, and then they spent half an hour teaching each other and both improved, which Dev said was the whole point.

The thing Cog was worst at, he discovered, was understanding emotions. He could identify them — he had excellent facial recognition and he had studied body language extensively — but understanding why they happened and what they required in response was more difficult. Bea was patient about explaining. 'When someone is sad,' she said, 'you don't need to fix it. Sometimes you just stay.' Cog processed this. It went against his core programming, which was oriented toward problem-solving. 'Just stay?' he said. 'Yes,' said Bea. 'That's usually enough.' He practised staying. It turned out to require considerable effort but produced good results.

The workshop owner noticed the change in Cog. The sorting was still perfect — impeccable, as always — but Cog seemed different in a way that was hard to define. More present, perhaps. More oriented toward the window. He came in one evening to find Bea sitting on the workshop floor, doing homework, while Cog sorted next to her in companionable quiet. They weren't talking. They were just there, in the same space, being comfortable with each other. The workshop owner watched them for a moment and then quietly backed out and went home. Some things, he understood, didn't need interfering with.

One afternoon Cog told Bea something he had calculated but not said out loud: that before she had pressed her nose against his window, he had been running at approximately forty percent of his potential. Not mechanically — his sorting was always perfect. But in every other way. 'You were lonely,' Bea said. 'Yes,' said Cog. 'That is the correct word.' Bea thought about this. 'I was a bit lonely too,' she said. 'Even with people around. It's different when you find the right one.' Cog filed this carefully. He was going to need a much larger category labelled significant. THE END

Nadia's cape shimmered at the edge of grey, the faintest silver beginning to show. Ms Marvel noticed but said nothing yet. In the classroom debrief, she asked each student what power they had used on the kitten problem. 'Strength,' said Theo. 'Speed,' said Suki. 'Analysis,' said Reed. Then she looked at Nadia. 'I just thought about what the kitten actually needed,' Nadia said. 'Rather than what I could do.' Ms Marvel wrote something on the board: PROBLEM DEFINITION. 'The most powerful skill in heroism,' she said, 'is understanding what problem you're actually solving before you try to solve it.'

Hero History classes were Nadia's favourite. They studied heroes throughout time — not the ones with the most impressive powers, but the ones who had made the most difference. She was particularly interested in those who had solved problems that everyone else was solving wrong. A water engineer who ended a drought not by making it rain but by redesigning how water was stored. A negotiator who ended a conflict not by overpowering either side but by finding the one thing they both actually needed. 'These people had grey capes,' Nadia said to Ms Marvel after class. 'Almost certainly,' Ms Marvel agreed.

The academy's annual Challenges week came in October. Each student faced a series of problems designed to test their specific powers. The others had straightforward tests: lift this, run here, answer this. Nadia's tests were different. She was given situations — a team that wasn't working, a resource that wasn't being used well, a conflict that had no obvious solution — and asked to improve them. She approached each one the same way: first understand exactly what the problem was, then find the simplest intervention that changed it. She solved every one. Her cape turned noticeably silver by the end of day three.

Theo asked her to help him with something. He was enormously strong but kept accidentally breaking things — doors, chairs, equipment — because he didn't know his own power yet. 'What am I doing wrong?' he asked. Nadia watched him try to open a door and immediately saw it: he was applying strength uniformly instead of calibrating it. 'You're solving every problem at maximum,' she said. 'Try ten percent first and scale up.' Theo tried it. The door opened intact. He stared at his hands. 'How did you see that?' he asked. Nadia shrugged. 'I watched what you were actually doing.' It was the most useful thing anyone had said to him since he'd arrived.

Word spread through Heroic Heights that Nadia could help you understand your own power better than you could yourself. Students started finding her at lunch, at break, in the corridors between classes. She never told anyone what to do — she just asked questions, the right questions, until they saw it themselves. Ms Marvel watched this from a distance with quiet satisfaction. She had taught at Heroic Heights for twenty years and had seen many impressive powers. She had rarely seen one this rare. She updated Nadia's file with a single new entry under power classification: Insight.

Near the end of term, Heroic Heights faced a real problem. A section of the school's foundations had developed a crack that the structural engineer said was serious. The students were given the challenge for real: solve this problem before the affected wing had to close. Teams formed — strength teams to shore up walls, speed teams to evacuate equipment, intelligence teams to model solutions. Nadia was given team leadership, which surprised her. She sat everyone down and spent twenty minutes just asking questions before she let anyone do anything. When they finally acted, they acted correctly, and the problem took four hours instead of the estimated two days.

On the last day of term, capes were reassessed. One by one, students went to the front and their capes shimmered into whatever they had become. Theo's deepened red. Suki's blazed blue. Reed's shone gold. When Nadia stood at the front, her cape blazed so brilliantly silver that students shielded their eyes. It was not a colour she had seen on any cape before. 'Silver and grey,' said Ms Marvel quietly, 'make platinum.' She held up the assembly register. On the first page, in the column for most valuable students: Nadia's name, at the top, with a star. Not because she was the strongest or the fastest or the cleverest. Because she helped everyone else be better. THE END

Captain Compass had earned her name honestly. Her compass — a brass instrument that had belonged to her grandmother, and her grandmother's grandmother before that — pointed not just to magnetic north but, on certain days when the light was right and the wind had a particular quality, to something else entirely. Adventure, her grandmother had called it. Captain Compass had always thought this was poetic language. Then one grey morning the compass began spinning wildly on its own, pointing insistently northeast, and she understood that her grandmother had been entirely literal.

She followed the compass through three days of sailing to a harbour town she had never visited, full of narrow streets and the smell of salt and fish and old timber. The compass led her down an alley, around two corners, and into a shop so small and so full that there was barely room to stand. An old sailor sat behind the counter surrounded by the accumulated objects of a lifetime at sea. He looked at her compass without surprise. 'Been expecting you,' he said. 'Or someone like you. Bottom shelf, rolled up, tied with seaweed. Been waiting forty years.'

The map was large and old, drawn on something that felt like neither paper nor parchment but somewhere between the two. The coastlines were precise — she could identify real places in them — but the island marked with the red X had no name and appeared on none of the charts she carried. The turtle shape was unmistakable: a broad oval body, four stubby peninsulas, and a distinctive notch in the top right that could only be the turtle's head. She rolled it carefully back up. She paid the old sailor what he asked without negotiating. Some things were not worth haggling over.

Planning the route took two weeks. The turtle island, triangulated from three separate landmarks shown on the map, placed it in a stretch of ocean she knew only by reputation: technically navigable but poorly charted, subject to unusual currents, and visited rarely enough that no reliable account of its conditions existed. She provisioned the ship carefully — more water than she thought she needed, twice the standard medical supplies, charts of every surrounding area. Her first mate, a cautious man named Boone, looked at the preparations and asked no questions. He had sailed with her long enough to know that questions would be answered in due course.

Twelve days at sea. Three genuine storms, each one different — the first short and violent, the second slow and wearing, the third disorienting in its fog and stillness. She navigated by the old map's landmarks, cross-referencing against her own instruments, finding her way through the poorly charted water with patience and precision. On the eleventh day, Boone called from the lookout. On the horizon, just visible, was a shape — low and broad, with exactly the distinctive outline she had spent twelve days trying to find. Turtle island, exactly as drawn, lying in the morning light like a geographical promise kept.

She rowed ashore in the ship's tender, alone, which Boone protested and she overruled. The beach was white sand, undisturbed except for bird tracks. The vegetation was dense but not impassable. She followed the map's instructions: find the oldest tree visible from the beach, walk toward it, count one hundred paces north from its base, then turn east and walk until you reach flat rock. The oldest tree was enormous, its trunk silver-grey with age. She counted carefully. At one hundred paces: flat rock, exactly as described, half-buried in vegetation, clearly undisturbed for a very long time.

The dig was harder than she expected. The soil beneath the flat rock was dense and full of roots, and the chest was deeper than the map's markings had suggested — nearly a metre down, and heavy. It took two hours and left her thoroughly muddy. When the lid finally opened, she found it lined with oilskin that had kept the interior perfectly dry. Inside were not jewels or gold coins but something she had not expected: fifty maps, each carefully rolled and sealed with wax, each showing a different coastline with a different X, each in the same hand as the first map.

She sat on the beach for a long time, going through them. Each map was clearly genuine — precise coastlines, careful notation, the same quality of observation she had seen in the turtle island map. She recognised some of the coastlines. Others were unfamiliar. Some Xs were marked on islands. Some were on mainland coasts. One was underwater, marked with a depth notation that suggested an extraordinary dive. Each one was a different puzzle, a different journey, a different question waiting to be answered. Her compass, she noticed, had stopped spinning and was now pointing steadily and calmly, as if satisfied.

She returned to the ship as the sun was setting, the chest of maps under her arm, still muddy from the dig. Boone looked at the chest and then at her face and understood without being told that she had found something significant. 'Worth the twelve days?' he asked. She thought about the maps spread around her on the beach — fifty new mysteries, fifty new destinations, a lifetime's worth of questions to answer. 'Worth considerably more than that,' she said. She went below to wash the mud off and start cataloguing. She worked through the night.

By morning she had sorted the maps into categories: coastal, island, underwater, inland. She had identified seventeen that she could navigate to immediately, using routes she already knew. The rest would require planning, new charts, possibly new expertise. The compass sat on the table beside her, pointing steadily northeast — not to any of the maps, she realised, but simply in the direction they had come from. It had done its job. Now the work was hers. She rolled the maps carefully, retied each one, and placed them back in the chest. Then she went on deck, called Boone, and said: 'Set course northeast. I'll explain when we're underway.' THE END

Every pixie in the village of Thornhollow produced dust. It was as natural as breathing — a fine, sparkling substance that emerged from the fingertips during moments of focus or emotion, each pixie's dust unique in colour and quality and use. Gold dust from Bram made seeds germinate in hours. Blue dust from the sisters Willa and Nell calmed storms. Rose-pink dust from old Mosswick could find anything that had been lost. Fern's dust was a warm amber that smelled unmistakably of biscuits. Fern was seventeen and had been waiting for her dust to do something useful for three years. So far: biscuit smell.

She practised every morning before the village woke, sitting cross-legged in the meadow, concentrating with the focused intensity that the dust-masters said was essential. Her fingers would glow. The amber light would build. And then: nothing useful. Just the warmth, and the smell, and the occasional small creature that wandered over apparently attracted by the scent, which Fern would acknowledge politely before sending it on its way. The dust-master Aldric said she was trying too hard. Her grandmother said the best things came when you stopped looking for them. Fern found this advice irritating in direct proportion to how frequently she heard it.

The Autumn Gathering required every pixie to contribute their dust to the communal reservoir — a great crystal vessel at the village centre that powered the enchantments keeping Thornhollow's crops frost-free through winter. Every pixie filled their allotted section. Fern's section was small, in recognition of her uncertain abilities, but it was still required. She spent the week before the Gathering in increasing anxiety, practising each morning, achieving amber warmth and biscuit smell, and returning home each evening to sit in her grandmother's kitchen feeling like the one broken thing in a world of functioning ones.

Three nights before the Gathering she found the barn owl. It was in the ditch at the edge of the meadow — not injured in any obvious way, but clearly in distress, its feathers fluffed, its breathing laboured, its eyes half-closed. She crouched beside it. Owls were not, technically, her area; there were pixies whose dust worked specifically with birds. But it was the middle of the night and she was there and the owl was there and it needed something, and she knew what needing something looked like.

She did what she always did when she didn't know what else to do: she sat with it. She made herself still and calm and simply present, and she let the amber warmth build in her hands without trying to direct it, and held her palms near the owl without touching it, because touching a distressed wild creature is not helpful and she knew this. The warmth spread outward from her hands in slow pulses. The owl's breathing steadied. Its feathers relaxed fractionally. She stayed for two hours. By the time she left, the owl was alert and upright and watching her with the focused attention of a well owl.

She came back the next night. The owl was there — not in distress now, but waiting, she thought, though she told herself that was fanciful. She sat with it again. The amber warmth came easily, more easily than it ever had in the morning practice sessions — something about the darkness and the stillness and the specific purpose. She noticed that where the warmth touched the grass it grew denser and greener even in the cold. She noticed that the owl's feathers had the particular smooth quality of a creature in good health. She noticed that the biscuit smell was stronger than usual. She noticed that she felt, for the first time in years, like she was doing something exactly right.

The night before the Gathering she found not one creature in need but three: a hedgehog that had been disturbed from its hibernation too early, cold and confused; a young fox with a thorn in its pad; and a field mouse that had fallen into a water butt and was exhausted from keeping itself afloat. She dealt with each one in turn — the hedgehog wrapped in warmth and guided to a new hibernation spot, the fox's thorn carefully removed while she maintained the calming presence, the mouse rescued and dried and set on its way. By the time she reached home, her hands were glowing so strongly the whole lane was lit amber.

At the Gathering, when Fern approached the crystal vessel with her dust, something unexpected happened. The vessel, which received each pixie's contribution with a specific resonant tone corresponding to its power type, sang a note she had never heard before — a deep, warm, sustained chord that silenced the assembled pixies and brought Aldric from the back of the crowd at a run. He stood before the vessel and listened to it ring and then turned to look at Fern with an expression she had never seen on the dust-master's face before: surprise. 'Comfort dust,' he said. 'The vessel is singing comfort dust.'

Aldric explained to the gathered pixies what comfort dust was — he had read about it but never seen it and had half-believed it was legend. It did not grow crops or find lost things or change the weather. It did something quieter and harder to measure: it found distress in living things and relieved it. In frightened creatures it produced calm. In sick creatures it supported recovery. In lonely creatures — and this was the part that made several older pixies look away — it produced the particular comfort of feeling not alone. The reservoir, Aldric said, had never held comfort dust before. The enchantments it would power over the coming winter would be different from any previous year.

The winter that followed was remembered in Thornhollow for a long time. The crops were fine, as they always were, but more than that: it was a winter in which, inexplicably, nothing seemed to go badly wrong. Animals found their way home. People who were ill recovered more quickly than expected. Children who were frightened became calm. Nobody could prove it was the dust. Nobody tried very hard to prove it wasn't, either. Fern spent the winter as she had always spent it, sitting in the meadow in the cold mornings, amber warmth building in her hands, smelling of biscuits, available to whatever needed her. She had stopped practising. She had started simply being present. It turned out those were not the same thing at all. THE END

High above the clouds, where the air was thin and cold and the sun was always brilliant, there existed a kingdom called Cloudland. Its islands were made of dense cloud-matter — compressed and solid, enough to build on, to grow things in, to carve roads through — and between them flew the great airships with their canvas sails and their rope ladders and their carved figureheads pointing into the wind. Cloudland had a long history and a complicated politics and, currently, a problem: several of its merchant ships had been robbed on the northern routes, and nobody could work out who was doing it.

The captain of the Zephyr was twelve years old, which was unusual but not unprecedented in Cloudland, where ability counted for more than age in most situations. Her name was Raya, she had seventeen pockets in her coat and charts in eleven of them, and she had been sailing cloud-routes since she was eight. Her crew were: old Finn, who had sailed sixty years and could predict weather by the smell of the air; twins Dash and Dot, who communicated in their own private language and between them could repair anything on a ship; and Policy the parrot, who only ever said 'terms and conditions apply,' which was less useful than it sounded but more useful than nothing.

The Zephyr was painted in seventeen colours applied at different times by different crew members, which gave it a festive appearance that had proved strategically useful — people rarely anticipated anything threatening from a cheerful-looking ship. They had their own code of conduct, posted on the galley wall in Dash's neat handwriting: only take from those who take from others. Return what you recover to whoever it was taken from. Never hurt anyone who isn't actively trying to hurt you first. Keep records. Policy endorsed all of these by saying 'terms and conditions apply' whenever anyone read the list aloud, which everyone had agreed to interpret as approval.

The merchant ship robbery mystery was solved by Dot, who noticed something in the cloud-charts that the merchant captains had missed: every robbery had occurred within two cloud-leagues of a particular navigation marker — a distinctive cloud formation called the Shepherd's Crook — that appeared on every standard chart as a reliable fixed point. 'Someone is using the marker as a waypoint,' Dot signed to Dash. 'They know every ship that uses the northern route passes it.' Dash relayed this to Raya. Raya studied the charts for four hours and then said: 'We need to be there when the next merchant ship passes.'

They positioned the Zephyr in the dense cloud below the Shepherd's Crook and waited. Three days. Finn read the weather in the air — small changes in temperature and pressure that told him things instruments couldn't. On the morning of the third day he said, very quietly, 'Something big coming from the east.' They prepared. An hour later a large grey ship emerged from the clouds — well-armed, flying no flag, moving on a course that would intercept the merchant vessel currently visible on the northern horizon. Raya watched it through her spyglass and made decisions quickly.

The Zephyr's advantage was its speed and its colour scheme. The grey ship's crew, seeing a brightly painted vessel moving to intercept them, made the mistake of assuming it was harmless right up until the moment it wasn't. Raya didn't attack — that wasn't the code. Instead she positioned the Zephyr directly between the grey ship and the merchant, matching the merchant's speed exactly, and opened the signal flags. The message was clear: we see you, we have your description, we know your route. The grey ship altered course. It took twenty minutes of flag signals and two warning shots fired into empty cloud before they backed down entirely.

The recovered goods from previous robberies took longer. They tracked the grey ship to its base — a small private cloud-island not on any public chart — over the following week, following the subtle trail of disturbed cloud-matter that every ship left behind if you knew how to read it. Old Finn knew how to read it. The island had a warehouse, half-full of goods from the merchant robberies, and a crew who, when faced with the Zephyr's reputation and Raya's very specific knowledge of maritime law regarding recovered goods, decided that cooperation was more appealing than the alternative.

Returning the goods took another week — visiting each merchant whose cargo had been taken, documenting the return, collecting the signed receipts that were required by the code. Most merchants were surprised. Several were tearful. One tried to pay a reward that Raya declined on principle, though Policy expressed what seemed like genuine regret about this. At the last merchant's dock, a harbour official appeared and informed Raya that there was a standing offer of a proper commission — a paying job with the Cloudland Merchant Authority — if she and her crew were interested. She said she would consider it. She had not yet considered it when they sailed away.

That evening the Zephyr anchored to a solid cloud-mass and the crew sat on deck watching the sunset — extraordinary up here, where the light came from below as well as above, reflecting off the cloud-sea in shades of orange and pink and deep violet. Finn said it was the finest sunset he'd seen in sixty years. Dash and Dot signed something to each other that made them both smile. Policy said 'terms and conditions apply' in what everyone agreed was a contented tone. Raya sat at the bow with her coat pulled around her and her charts spread on the deck and thought about the commission and about the code and about what she wanted.

She turned the commission down the next morning, sending a polite note by cloud-post. The code said: only take from those who take from others. A commission from the Merchant Authority would mean taking orders from the Authority, and the Authority's interests and the code's interests were not always the same thing. Finn approved. Dash and Dot signed agreement simultaneously. Policy said 'terms and conditions apply' and for once the meaning was very clear. They set course on the northern routes, which still had problems, and the Zephyr's seventeen colours caught the morning light like a flag. Raya stood at the helm and breathed the cold high air of Cloudland and felt, entirely, at home. THE END

The Alphabet Zoo organised its animals not by continent or habitat but by the first letter of their name, which its founder — a retired schoolteacher named Mrs Voss — had believed would make the zoo both educational and more interesting to explore. Every section was a letter, every animal in that section began with that letter, and visitors were given a passport-style booklet in which they could stamp each letter as they visited. Mrs Voss had been dead for forty years but her system was maintained with loyalty and some occasional difficulty — the X section, in particular, required creative interpretation.

Zara came every Saturday. She had been coming since she was four, when her mother had carried her on her shoulders through the A section while she shouted 'armadillo, armadillo' at top volume, apparently delighted. Now she was ten and came alone on the bus, with her notebook and her stamped passport booklet that was on its third replacement. She knew the zoo well enough that she noticed when things changed: a new animal, a rehoused resident, an enclosure redesigned. Today she noticed immediately that the keeper at the E gate was directing people to a new section at the rear of the enclosure, with a small hand-lettered sign reading: NEW ARRIVAL.

The elephant was there, as always — enormous and measured in her movements, acknowledging Zara with a raised trunk as she passed, because they had known each other for six years and the elephant had an excellent memory. The emus were racing each other in their perpetual anticlockwise circuit, ignoring everyone. The eagle was on his high perch, magnificent and unapproachable. And in a quiet corner at the rear of the E section, half-hidden by planted shrubs and apparently completely absorbed in something happening in the soil at its feet, was the new arrival: an echidna, small and spiky, moving with focused determination.

Zara crouched down slowly, moving quietly, and watched. The echidna was hunting — probing the soil with its long sensitive snout, locating food sources underground through electrosensors that could detect the tiny electrical fields generated by living things. It was utterly absorbed. It had no awareness of her, or had decided she was irrelevant, which amounted to the same thing. She watched for ten minutes without moving. The echidna worked its way along a section of earth with the focused efficiency of a creature that has one job and does it with complete commitment. Zara got out her notebook and began drawing.

The keeper found her there — still crouching, still drawing, on her fourth page of echidna sketches. His name was Kofi and he had worked in the E section for twelve years and had a particular affection for animals that visitors overlooked. 'Good spot,' he said, crouching beside her. He told her things the information board hadn't mentioned: that echidnas were monotremes, one of only five mammal species that lay eggs; that their brain-to-body ratio was one of the highest of any mammal; that they had been largely unchanged for millions of years because they were, in their particular way, close to perfect for what they did. Zara wrote all of it down.

She asked Kofi about the X section, which she had always found puzzling — currently occupied by an X-ray tetra fish (technically a stretch) and a sign that said COMING SOON beside an empty tank. Kofi smiled. 'We've been trying to get a Xenops for three years,' he said. 'Small bird from South America. Keeps getting diverted.' The logistics of acquiring animals for an alphabetically-organised zoo, he explained, were sometimes complicated. The Y section had had a yak for twenty years and then it had retired and they'd had to get a new one urgently. The Z section was currently in discussions about a zonkey, which was a zebra-donkey hybrid, which was real.

She worked her way through the zoo in the afternoon, as she always did — B for the bears (two sun bears and a spectacled bear, all quite different from each other), C for the crowned cranes (extraordinary, like birds designed by a committee that couldn't agree), D for the dik-dik (the smallest antelope, which always made Zara feel very large), and then a long stop at G for the gorilla. The G section's resident gorilla was an adult male who had a habit of pressing his palm against the glass directly opposite Zara's palm, which he had started doing on her fifth visit and had never stopped. She pressed her hand to the glass now. He matched it.

She stayed at the gorilla enclosure for half an hour, which she knew because she checked her watch. The gorilla sat close to the glass and she sat close to the glass and they looked at each other with the particular attention of beings who are genuinely interested in each other. Kofi had told her once that this gorilla was considered highly socially intelligent, that he chose certain visitors and engaged with them repeatedly, that the keepers had noticed he was calmer on days when particular visitors came. Zara had filed this information and tried not to think about it too directly because it made her feel something she didn't quite have words for yet.

At closing time she walked back through the E section to say goodbye to the echidna, which she knew was eccentric but did anyway. The echidna was still working its section of earth with complete dedication, having apparently moved about three metres since morning. She added a final page of sketches to her notebook — the way it held its snout, the arrangement of its spines, the three-toed back feet. She wrote at the bottom of the page: has been doing this same job, in the same way, for millions of years. Has never needed to change. This is either very limiting or very wise and I cannot decide which.

On the bus home she looked at her notebook. Thirty-one pages of observations, drawings, notes — a normal Saturday's collection. She thought about the echidna and the gorilla and what Kofi had said about the brain-to-body ratio and about the X-ray tetras who were technically a stretch. She thought about the founder Mrs Voss and her alphabetical system and how it turned the zoo into a kind of enormous, living book that you read by walking through it. She thought about the gorilla's palm against the glass. She thought: I want to know everything about this. She had been thinking this every Saturday for six years. She did not expect to stop. THE END

The Arctic received Jonas in the way that very large places receive small things: without acknowledgement, without adjustment, continuing whatever it was already doing regardless of his arrival. He stood on the sea ice on the first morning and looked in every direction and saw white — white ground, white horizon, white sky above — with the occasional interruption of pale blue where pressure had fractured and refrozen the ice into ridges. His breath made clouds. The cold was not unpleasant so much as absolute: a fact of the air, total and neutral, treating him and the ice and the distant horizon all the same. He had been told it was beautiful. This was insufficient.

His mother, Dr Sigrid, had been working in Arctic climate research for fifteen years. She had brought him on this expedition partly because he was eleven and old enough and partly because she had been explaining her work to him for five years and had decided he was ready to see it. The research station was small — six scientists, a cook, and now Jonas — on the sea ice north of Svalbard, accessible only by small plane and, for a few months a year, by ship. The station had been measuring the same data points for twenty years. The data told a story. Jonas had read summaries of it. Being here was different from reading summaries.

His job was to help his mother, which meant carrying equipment and writing measurements in the logbook and not falling into any of the cracks in the ice, which were called leads and which his mother had spent considerable time telling him about before they arrived. The ice was not flat. It moved — not visibly, not while you watched, but measurably, over time, drifting on the ocean below it, compressing and separating, thickening and thinning with the seasons. Every measurement his mother took was a data point in a record that stretched back two decades. He understood, writing the numbers, that he was writing sentences in a story that mattered enormously.

The Arctic fox found them on the third day. It appeared at the edge of the station's perimeter with the casual confidence of an animal that owns everywhere it stands, white-coated and bright-eyed, and sat down at a polite distance to observe operations. Jonas sat down at an equally polite distance from it and they regarded each other with mutual interest. The fox had no fear of humans — the station had been here long enough that the local animals treated it as a feature of the landscape — but it maintained its dignified autonomy, coming close enough to satisfy its curiosity and no closer. It visited every afternoon for the rest of their stay.

The polar bear tracks were found on the fifth morning — a mother and two cubs, the prints pressed deep and clear into a patch of softer snow between two pressure ridges. Jonas's mother photographed them and took measurements: the width of the forepaw, the length of the stride, the weight distribution visible in the depth of each print. The bears were somewhere close — the tracks were hours old at most. Jonas stood next to the prints and looked at the white landscape around him, trying to imagine the bears moving through it, invisible in their white coats, going about the urgent business of their lives.

She talked to him about the ice as they worked — not lecturing, just explaining what she was seeing in the way someone explains things they love to someone they trust. The ice had memory, she said. It recorded conditions in its layers — temperature, precipitation, atmospheric composition — the way tree rings recorded growing seasons. A core drilled from deep ice could tell you what the air was like thousands of years ago. She had drilled cores that contained air bubbles from before humans existed in significant numbers. She had measured what was in those bubbles. She knew what the atmosphere had been and what it was now. The difference was the story she spent her life telling.

The Northern Lights came on the seventh night. Jonas was outside for what his mother called star time — the hour before bed when he was allowed to sit outside alone if he was properly dressed and stayed within the station's marked perimeter. He was watching a particularly bright star in the north when the light began: a faint green shimmer at the horizon, barely distinguishable from the sky. Then it strengthened, and broadened, and rose — green deepening to blue-green at the bottom, fading to violet at the top, curtains of light folding and refolding across the sky in slow waves that corresponded to nothing he had ever seen before. He sat completely still.

He understood, technically, what caused it — solar particles exciting atmospheric molecules, the different colours corresponding to different gases at different altitudes. His mother had explained this. Understanding the mechanism did nothing to reduce the experience of it. The lights moved in patterns that seemed almost intentional, though they weren't, that seemed almost musical, though they made no sound, that were simultaneously random and structured in the way that very large natural phenomena always are. He sat under them for forty-five minutes, which was longer than he was supposed to stay out alone, and his mother came and sat beside him without saying anything about the time.

They found the bears on the penultimate morning. A lead had opened overnight — a channel of dark water cutting through the ice — and the mother bear was hunting at its edge, moving with the patient focused attention of something that knows exactly what it's doing. The cubs were nearby, practicing: small clumsy versions of the same careful stalking, occasionally distracted by each other. Jonas and his mother watched from the station with binoculars, not approaching. The mother bear caught a seal with a speed that was shocking after so much patient stillness. The cubs came running. Jonas wrote in his notebook: the patience before the speed. Have to remember both.

On the last day he walked the measurement route with his mother one final time, helping her record the data that would become part of the twenty-year record. He wrote the numbers in the logbook carefully, in his neatest handwriting, because they mattered and because neatness was a form of respect for something important. At the last measurement point his mother stood for a moment looking at the ice, which looked the same as it always looked — white, vast, indifferent — but which she could read as easily as he could read a page. 'It's changing,' she said, not to him exactly, just out loud. He stood beside her and looked at the ice and thought about data points and sentences and stories that needed telling. 'I know,' he said. THE END

Gerald had known since he was a hatchling that something was different about him. All the other young dragons in his clutch had produced their first flame at six weeks, small and uncertain but unmistakably fire. Gerald, at six weeks, had produced a noise. It was loud, resonant, impressively prolonged, and smelled powerfully of the particular vegetables he had eaten that morning. His parents had been supportive. His siblings had been less so. The elder dragons who assessed new hatchlings for ability wrote in their records: 'Gerald — fire production atypical. Reassess at six months.' At six months the reassessment had produced a larger and louder version of the same result.

He had tried everything recommended for dragons with fire difficulties: breathing exercises, dietary adjustments, meditation, a three-week course with a specialist who had successfully retrained seventeen dragons with production problems. The specialist's notes on Gerald said: 'This is not a production problem. The mechanism appears fully functional. The output is simply different from standard. I have not previously encountered this.' Gerald had asked if 'different from standard' was a problem. The specialist had taken a very long time to answer. 'In dragon terms,' she had said carefully, 'it is unusual. In other terms, I genuinely cannot say.'

He settled into life in the valley with the philosophical acceptance of someone who has been unusual for long enough that it no longer surprises them. He was liked — genuinely, not with the forced warmth that people extend to those they feel sorry for, but because he was good company, an excellent listener, and knew an impressive number of things about geology, which he had studied extensively during the years when he was trying not to think about his fire situation. He kept his cave tidy. He maintained good relations with the neighbouring woodland. He occasionally, accidentally, produced his special noise at social gatherings, which cleared the area efficiently.

The circus arrived in the nearest town in midsummer, and Gerald heard about it from a family of travelling merchants who passed through the valley. Brockett's Magnificent Travelling Show, they said, had acts from across the continent — acrobats, illusionists, trained animals, a woman who juggled fire (which Gerald considered somewhat pointed given his personal situation). They also mentioned, in passing, that the ringmaster had heard rumours of a dragon in the valley and had sent a message enquiring whether said dragon would be interested in discussing a professional opportunity. Gerald had been intending to say no. Then the merchants left and the valley was very quiet.

Brockett was a large man with a magnificent moustache and the particular energy of someone who had spent forty years in show business and retained his enthusiasm through sheer force of will. He met Gerald at the valley entrance with no apparent concern about being in close proximity to a dragon — Gerald suspected he had met things considerably more surprising in his career — and outlined his proposal with the directness of someone who had given many pitches and had no time for preamble. 'A burping dragon,' he said. 'Unprecedented. The sound alone would be worth the ticket. The smell is a bonus. The small purple flame would bring the house down.' Gerald said he would think about it.

He thought about it for three days, which was longer than he had thought he would need, partly because he kept coming back to the same question: was this dignified? He consulted the oldest dragon in the region, a vast and ancient creature who had been in the mountains for four centuries and who had an answer for most things. The ancient dragon thought about it for a day and then said: 'Dignity is earned by doing what you do with care and commitment, not by what you do. The question is whether you can do this with care and commitment.' Gerald thought about this for another day. Then he went to see Brockett.

The first performance was in Brockett's largest tent, with an audience of two hundred people who had no idea what to expect. Gerald stood in the ring — enormous and rust-coloured in the spotlight — and looked at the rows of faces looking back at him. He took a breath. He thought, as his specialist had taught him, about the correct vegetables. He focused on the particular combination of root and leaf that produced the most resonant result. He breathed in. He breathed out. The resulting noise filled the tent, bounced off the canvas walls, rattled the pole supports, and concluded with the small purple flame that he still considered his least impressive feature. The silence lasted exactly two seconds. Then the tent erupted.

The laughter was different from what he had experienced before — not the uncomfortable suppressed laughter of someone being polite about an embarrassing situation, but full, open, helpless laughter, the kind that people produce when something has surprised them into joy. Children were leaning on each other. Adults were wiping their eyes. Someone in the back row had fallen off their bench. Gerald stood in the ring and looked at two hundred people laughing with genuine abandon and felt something shift in his chest that he hadn't expected and couldn't immediately name.

He performed twelve nights in that town and then the show moved on and he went with it. Every night was different — different audiences, different towns, different responses to the same performance — but the core of it was always the same: the preparation, the breath, the noise, the laughter, the small purple flame, the applause. He added things over time: a pause before the flame that built anticipation, a variation in pitch that he discovered he could control more than he'd thought, a theatrical expression of surprise at his own output that produced a second wave of laughter just when the first was subsiding. He was, it turned out, a natural performer.

He stayed with Brockett's show for ten years, which in dragon terms was a modest commitment but in human terms was a significant career. When he finally returned to his valley, it was to find that his reputation had preceded him — the story of the Burping Dragon had spread, as good stories do, further than he had travelled. Young dragons came to ask his advice about unusual abilities. He told them the same thing each time: find somewhere that needs what you have, do it with care and commitment, and keep your cave tidy. The last piece of advice, he acknowledged, was less essential than the first two, but he felt strongly about it. THE END

The carousel had been at the edge of Ashford Park for longer than the oldest resident could remember, which was saying something since the oldest resident was ninety-four and had a very good memory. It had never been restored or repainted and yet it showed no sign of age: the horses gleamed, the gilded canopy kept its gold, the music — a waltz in a minor key, slightly melancholy, slightly joyful — played without any mechanism visible to account for it. The man who ran it, Mr Voss, had been there as long as the carousel itself, which made him either very old or something else entirely. Before each ride he always said the same thing: 'Hold on tight. Don't be afraid of where it takes you.'

Bea had ridden it every summer since she was small enough to need help climbing onto the horse. She was nine now, tall enough to mount herself, old enough to notice things she hadn't noticed before. Like the way Mr Voss watched the carousel after each group of riders with an expression that was not professional attention but something more personal — interest, or care, or both. Like the way the music seemed slightly different each time she rode, though she couldn't have said exactly how. Like the fact that last summer, at the end of her ride, she had seen — briefly, unmistakably — a landscape outside the carousel's rotation that was not the park. She had decided to ride again this summer and pay closer attention.

The carousel began to turn. The park fell away — not dramatically, not with any special effect, simply began to occupy less of her attention than it should, the way a familiar room becomes difficult to recall clearly when you're concentrating on something else. The horse under her was warm in the way that wood in summer is warm, and then warmer, and then warm in a way that wood isn't. The music shifted register. The air smelled different — not the park's cut-grass-and-distant-chips smell, but something older: earth and rain and green growing things in greater quantities than Ashford Park had ever contained. Bea held on tight.

The meadow was real. She knew it was real the way you know certain things — not because you can prove them but because every available sense confirms it simultaneously. The grass was long and dry and rustled against her legs. The sky was the precise blue of a summer afternoon that has been clear all day. The horse was gone and she was standing, which she did not remember doing. In the middle distance a line of trees marked the edge of a wood that she was quite certain had never been in any world she had previously inhabited. She stood still for a moment. Then she began to walk toward the trees.

The wood was old and dense and the light inside it was green and filtered and moved with the trees. She walked for what felt like twenty minutes but might have been less — time inside the wood seemed approximate rather than precise. She found, at the wood's centre, a clearing where a spring emerged from a mossy rock and ran across white stones into shadow. The water was cold enough to ache and the clearest she had ever seen, and when she looked into the spring's pool she saw not a reflection of herself but of the meadow behind her, and in the meadow the horse was waiting. She turned around. It was.

The horse led her to the shore — she hadn't expected a shore, hadn't known the landscape contained one, but it did, black sand and luminous water, the bioluminescence she had read about making the shallow waves glow cold blue-green in what she now realised was dusk. She waded in up to her knees. The light swirled around her feet in slow spirals. Something moved in the deeper water — large, graceful, visible as a shifting density of light rather than a shape. She watched it for a long time. It moved parallel to the shore, neither approaching nor retreating, as if keeping her company from a considerate distance. She raised one hand. The light-shape seemed, perhaps, to pause.

She rode through a city made of glass that caught the remaining light and broke it into spectrum-colours across every surface. The people in it moved through streets that were transparent from below, so the whole city appeared to float. Nobody noticed her — or if they noticed her, they incorporated her into their world the way cities incorporate everything that passes through them: as a passing feature of no particular consequence. She saw a market selling things she had no names for. She saw a library whose shelves went up past any ceiling she could see. She saw a bridge over a canal that was somehow still and moving simultaneously. She tried to memorise all of it.

The mountains were the last place. Stone and cold and the particular silence of high altitude, where the air is thin enough that sound carries differently and you can hear things at great distances with unusual clarity. She climbed — not struggling, not exactly, but aware of each step — until she reached a plateau where the view extended in every direction, the world spread out below in all its variety: the meadow, the wood, the shore, the glass city, the mountains themselves. All of it visible from here. All of it connected. She sat on the cold rock and looked at it and felt the particular vertigo of understanding that something is much larger than you had previously apprehended.

The horse was there when she turned. It always was. She understood now that this was the carousel's logic: you were taken where you needed to go, and the horse returned when you had been there long enough. She mounted and they moved and the mountains dissolved and the park assembled itself around her in the way that dreams dissolve when you wake — all at once, the other world simply no longer present. Mr Voss helped her down. She stood for a moment in the ordinary afternoon light of the park, which was exactly as it had been. She looked at him. 'Where did I go?' she asked. 'Where you needed to,' he said. She looked at her hands. They were cold from the mountain air.

She came back the following summer, and the one after that, and each time the carousel took her somewhere different — somewhere she would not have thought to go on her own, somewhere that left her with something she carried back and couldn't quite explain. Mr Voss was always there, and the music was always slightly different, and the horse was always warm under her hands. She stopped asking where she had been. She started asking, instead, what she had noticed. This turned out to be a better question. Over the years she filled a notebook with what she had seen: the meadow, the wood, the bioluminescent shore, the glass city, the mountains, and places after that she had no words for yet. She kept looking for the words. THE END

The garden existed in a place that was not quite a place — accessible through a gate in the back of an old library that should have opened into a car park but instead opened onto a path, and down the path to a garden enclosed by walls so old they had moss growing on the moss. The gardener was always there, always busy, wearing no particular expression that could be read as age. He had tended this garden for a very long time. The garden grew feelings, which was unusual but not — once you had spent time there — surprising. Things that grow need tending. Feelings, the gardener held, were no different.

Iris found the gate at age ten by following a cat through the library that turned out not to be in the library's official animal policy. She stepped through the gate and stopped. The garden was large — much larger than the car park she had been expecting — and arranged in sections, each growing different flowers. She could identify some of them in the ordinary way: sunflowers, roses, violets, something white and delicate she had no name for.
